display_title: The Ancient Roots of Our Gut Bacteria
display_title_he: השורשים העתיקים של חיידקי המעיים שלנו
short_summary: New research reveals that indigenous populations in Tanzania and Bolivia share a nearly identical gut microbiome, suggesting these bacteria have evolved alongside humans for millennia.

sources.name: NPR
sources.title: Gut microbes followed migrating humans across continents, new study suggests

paragraphs: A groundbreaking study published in the journal Nature has unveiled a profound connection between two isolated populations living thousands of miles apart. Researchers meticulously analyzed the gut microbiomes of the Hadza hunter-gatherers in northern Tanzania and the Tsimane horticulturalists in the Bolivian Amazon. Despite the vast geographical divide and distinct dietary habits, these communities exhibit a startling 90% overlap in their gut bacteria, sharing approximately 1,200 identical species. This discovery suggests that our gut flora is not merely a collection of random environmental acquisitions, but a legacy of our shared human history.

Scientists posit that this microbial kinship originated with common ancestors in Africa. Long before human migration dispersed these groups, specific bacteria were transmitted through generations. As humans traversed Eurasia and eventually crossed the land bridge connecting Russia to Alaska, these microbes accompanied them. When rising sea levels submerged this bridge, the physical isolation made it nearly impossible for these populations to exchange bacteria through traditional contact. Using dating techniques based on bacterial mutation rates, researchers determined that these microbial strains likely shared a common ancestor roughly 17,000 years ago.

Justin Sonnenburg, a professor at Stanford University and the study’s senior author, emphasizes that these microbes are co-evolved partners. These organisms assist in digestion, secrete molecules into the bloodstream, and influence immune responses and mood regulation. Crucially, the study reveals that about 60% of the microbes shared by the Hadza and Tsimane are rare or entirely absent in individuals living in industrialized, urban environments. This shift suggests that modern lifestyles have fundamentally altered our internal ecosystems.

This discrepancy raises urgent questions regarding the biological consequences of losing ancestral microbes. Sonnenburg argues that human genomes may have evolved to expect specific microbial functions, and their absence could contribute to the rise of inflammatory diseases. While the exact health implications remain a subject of intense investigation, the evidence indicates that our modern microbiome has diverged significantly from its ancestral state.

Experts caution that while the hypothesis is compelling, the field is still in its infancy. Andrew Moeller, an evolutionary biologist at Princeton University, notes that it remains unclear whether the loss of these ancestral taxa is inherently harmful or simply an adaptation to an industrialized lifestyle. Nevertheless, documenting these changes is a vital step toward understanding the complex relationship between human evolution and the microscopic organisms inhabiting our bodies. As scientists continue to map the history of our gut flora, they aim to identify which microbes are essential for long-term health and whether it is possible to restore the biodiversity lost to the modern world.

facts.fact: A study published in Nature compared the gut microbiomes of the Hadza people in Tanzania and the Tsimane people in Bolivia.
The two groups share approximately 1,200 bacterial species, representing a 90% overlap in their gut microbiomes.
Researchers suggest these microbes have been transmitted through generations since before human ancestors migrated out of Africa.
Around 60% of these shared ancestral microbes are rare or absent in the microbiomes of people living industrialized, modern lifestyles.
Microbiologists hypothesize that the loss of these ancestral microbes due to modern living may contribute to inflammatory diseases.
